primitives.name: Inhibition-Effective Reaction Potential
primitives.verbatim_quote: The net amount of functioning inhibitory potential resulting from a sequence of reaction evocations is a positircly accelerated function of the amount of work (W) inrolved in the performance of the response in question.
primitives.assumptions: Work is directly proportional to muscular effort; inhibition accumulates non-linearly with repeated responses.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When W approaches zero, \(\Delta I_n \to 0\); when c → 1, behavior becomes linearly dependent on work.

layer2.mapping: GSE state transition kernel encodes inhibition as a decreasing utility function over time, while GSI infers latent inhibition levels from observed response patterns.
layer2.telemetry: Mean inhibition per reinforcement, measured via reaction time variance during extinction trials.

primitives.name: Mean Net Inhibition Increment
primitives.verbatim_quote: It is evident that the mean net increment of inhibition per reinforcement must be the net inhibition divided by the number of reaction evocations.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'\\bar{\\Delta I}': 'mean net inhibition increment (dimensionless)', '\\Delta I': 'total net inhibition (dimensionless)', 'n': 'number of reaction evocations (unitless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Each reaction contributes equally to total inhibition; no external interference affects individual evocations.
primitives.breakdown_regime: As n increases, \(\bar{\Delta I}\) asymptotically decreases unless inhibition is externally modulated.

layer2.mapping: GSI uses \(\bar{\Delta I}\) as a sufficient statistic for estimating agent fatigue in sequential decision-making tasks.
layer2.telemetry: Average latency increase per trial in extinction protocol.

primitives.name: Accumulated Inhibition Function
primitives.verbatim_quote: Three comparable groups of albino rats were trained on a Skinner type of apparatus to press a bar for food
primitives.assumptions: Inhibition builds cumulatively under unreinforced conditions; functional form reflects mechanical work-to-inhibitory conversion.
primitives.breakdown_regime: At high W, saturation occurs due to biological limits on inhibition capacity.

layer2.mapping: GSE simulates behavioral decay using \(I_r(W)\) as a dynamic resistance term in action-value update rules.
layer2.telemetry: Cumulative reaction delay in extinction sessions.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core concept of inhibition-effective reaction potential emerges from the interplay between physical effort and behavioral suppression. Starting with the premise that work (W) drives inhibition, we derive a power-law relationship where inhibition accelerates with increasing effort. This is formalized as \(\Delta I_n = B \cdot W^{c}\), where c > 1 implies positive acceleration. The mean net increment \(\bar{\Delta I} = \Delta I / n\) normalizes this across repetitions, enabling statistical inference about average suppression per event. The accumulated inhibition function \(I_r(W)\) extends this into continuous space, integrating instantaneous inhibition rates over work. These primitives are foundational for modeling how organisms adapt behaviorally under fatigue or lack of reward. Dualities arise in that higher effort leads to stronger suppression but also reduces future responsiveness—this creates a feedback loop in both GSI's probabilistic inference and GSE’s deterministic state evolution. Failure modes include overfitting to early trials or assuming constant c, which can misrepresent adaptation dynamics. The system exhibits singularity when W approaches zero or when c approaches unity, indicating loss of sensitivity or linearity respectively.
